amendments.rule: Reordered or discontinuous target tokens may occupy one unit when they realize one source item. Do not absorb unrelated intervening words into that unit. **Where English repeats one source function word because its scope is distributed across coordinated or emphatically repeated phrases or clauses, every English occurrence belongs to that source morpheme's one possibly discontinuous unit.** `מִן` in `מִבּוֹא בְדָמִים וְהוֹשֵׁוַע` → *from bloodguiltiness, and from avenging* takes both occurrences of *from*, while the waw takes only *and*; `בִּי אֲנִי` → *upon me ... upon me* gives both occurrences of *upon* to the single preposition while the suffix and explicit pronoun take their respective *me*. The repeated English word is neither `added` nor reassigned to a neighboring source item merely to make the units contiguous. **An explicit personal pronoun is read the same way where the ASV resumes it in a later clause of the same verse.** Where a following verbless clause writes no subject of its own and the ASV supplies the subject pronoun that an explicit `הוּא`, `הֵמָּה`, `אֲנִי` or the like standing earlier in the verse denotes, both occurrences belong to that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, exactly as rule 18 gives both pronouns of a twice-rendered suffix to the suffix and rule 20 gives both halves of an identifying formula to its one `הוּא`: `הֵמָּה סֹחֲרֵי יָדֵךְ ... בָּם סֹחֲרָיִךְ` → *they were the merchants of thy hand ... in these were* ***they*** *thy merchants* gives both *they*s to the one `הֵמָּה`, headed on the first. Such a pronoun is not `added`, and it does not join the predicate's unit: rule 20 hands the predicate the construction's copula and, in a presentative clause, its dummy *there*, and a referential pronoun is neither, so the clause's supplied *were* goes to the predicate while the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it. This governs a clause with no subject of its own: where a finite verb stands in the resumed clause it takes the English subject pronoun under rule 17, which is a pronoun realizing that verb's own person and number. **And where the Hebrew stands the pronoun is not part of the condition.** Hebrew postposes an explicit subject pronoun after its predicate and that predicate's adjuncts, often before a coordinated second subject, while English writes a subject before its verb; where the ASV writes the pronoun in both places it has realized one written morpheme twice, and both occurrences are that pronoun's one discontinuous unit, headed on the first English occurrence: `וְהִנֵּה נִצָּב עַל־עֹלָתוֹ הוּא וְכָל־שָׂרֵי מוֹאָב` → *and lo* ***he*** *was standing by his burnt offering,* ***he*** *and all the princes of Moab* gives both *he*s to the one `הוּא`, while `נִצָּב` keeps the *was standing* rule 20 leaves it and the coordinated subject keeps its own English. So read whether one written pronoun is realized twice rather than which side of the resumption it stands on, and do not hand the first occurrence to the predicate to make the units contiguous: rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing a finite verb's own person and number, and a participle or other predicate morpheme in a verbless clause takes only the copula. **And the morpheme that denotes the resumed subject need not be a pronoun.** Where a common noun or a proper name written in the verse is the referent the ASV resumes, every English realization of that referent belongs to the noun's one possibly discontinuous unit on exactly the terms above, headed on the first English occurrence: `עַל־אֱלוֹהַּ נוֹרָא הוֹד` → ***God*** *hath upon* ***him*** *terrible majesty* gives both *God* and *him* to the one `אֱלוֹהַּ`, and `שַׁדַּי לֹא־מְצָאנֻהוּ שַׂגִּיא־כֹּחַ` → *Touching* ***the Almighty****, we cannot find him out;* ***He*** *is excellent in power* gives the resuming *He* to `שַׁדַּי`, while `שַׂגִּיא` keeps the *is excellent* rule 20 leaves it. This is the preceding paragraphs' own reasoning read for the morpheme that is actually written — the pronoun goes to the morpheme that denotes it — since what licenses the English word is that the verse writes the referent, and not the part of speech the ASV first realized it by. Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **And where the two realizations are not of the same kind, the head goes to the one writing the noun's own lexeme, whichever of them stands first.** The direction to head on the first English occurrence settles a tie between realizations of one kind — two *he*s, two *from*s, or a noun and the pronoun resuming it in that order — and it is not a preference for the phrase's left edge. Where the ASV realizes one written nominal both by a pronoun and by the word that writes its lexeme, rule 24 governs and the head is the lexeme-bearing word, exactly as rule 18 heads a twice-written suffix on the pronoun that realizes it directly rather than on the generic noun beside it, and as rule 31 keeps a head off a word the ASV supplied. This reaches a construct chain whose *nomen rectum* the ASV promotes to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's own relation as a possessive on the head noun: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף יַשְׁחִת רֵעֵהוּ` → *With* ***his*** *mouth* ***the godless man*** *destroyeth his neighbor* gives both *his* and *the godless man* to the one `חָנֵף`, headed on *godless*, while `פֶּה` keeps its own *mouth*, and `וּבְהַוַּת בֹּגְדִים יִלָּכֵדוּ` → *But* ***the treacherous*** *shall be taken in* ***their own*** *iniquity* divides the same way, headed on *treacherous*. Such a possessive is not `added` under rule 18's closing sentence and the promoted subject is not `added` under rule 17: a morpheme in the phrase answers to each, which is the count the paragraph above runs. Read which English word writes the lexeme before reaching for the first occurrence, since Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English writes the possessive before it, so the pronoun stands first as often as not. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amendments.why: PRO.11.6 and PRO.11.9 are one construction the chapter met twice: the ASV promotes a construct chain's nomen rectum to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's relation as a possessive on the head noun, so one written noun is realized twice ('the treacherous ... their own iniquity', 'his mouth ... the godless man'). Rule 25's resumed-noun paragraph already places both realizations in the rectum's one discontinuous unit, and rule 19 already gives the relational expression to the rectum, so nothing new is needed there. What the rule had not considered is the head. Both of its worked examples put the lexeme-bearing word first, so 'headed on the first English occurrence' and rule 24's cross-language anchor coincide; PRO.11.9 pulls them apart, because Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English fronts the possessive, leaving 'his' first and 'godless' second. Read literally the rule sends the head to 'his', which contradicts rule 24's own definition of a target head and rule 31's refusal to head on a word carrying no lexeme. The amendment states the boundary where it stands rather than adding a rule pointing back at it, and it closes the two related traps in the same breath: neither the fronted possessive nor the promoted subject is 'added', since a morpheme in the phrase answers to each. Both PRO.11 verses already head on the lexeme, so no patch follows from it; the correction is for the chapters after this one. Nothing else in rule 25 is changed.

conventions: Where a verbless colon writes a resultative lamed with its noun and the ASV supplies a whole lexical verb before it, the supplied verb, together with any subject or object supplied alongside it, is `added` under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb clause, and the preposition keeps only the bare word the ASV wrote for it: PRO.11.19 *shall attain* beside lamed to *unto*, PRO.11.19 *doeth it* beside lamed to *to*, and PRO.11.24 *it tendeth* beside lamed to *to*. Rule 49's resultative frame was the competing reading in each and is named in the verse notes; it was set aside because dropping the English verb leaves the preposition's own result relation still stated by *unto* or *to*, and because each supplied verb introduces an event, an agent or a dummy subject the Hebrew never wrote, which is rule 20's own boundary between a construction-supplied linking verb and a supplied lexical one.

The restrictive particle 'akh takes the *only* the ASV writes beside it and is not a home for a second connective, so the adversative *but* standing in the same colon at PRO.11.24 and the italic *But* opening the second colon at PRO.11.23 are each their own `added` unit under rule 14's closing sentences. The PRO.11.24 case is the contestable one and was decided deliberately: the ASV prints that *but* in roman while italicising the *it tendeth* beside it, but under rules 7 and 42 the absence of an italic is not evidence against an `added`, and giving 'akh both *but* and *only* would make one particle carry two English words doing two offices, which rule 51 refuses for a waw.

A possessive the ASV writes where no genitive relation and no suffix stands behind it is `added` under rule 18's closing sentence, and both instances here carry the ASV's own italic: *his* on tiqvah at PRO.11.7 and *their* on derekh at PRO.11.20. A possessive the English verb's fixed idiom requires is not that, and stays inside the verb's single rendering rather than falling to rule 44's supplied-possessive sentence: charesh to *holdeth his peace* at PRO.11.12 is one unit headed on *peace*, on the reasoning rule 30 gives for na' to *I beseech thee*, since English does not write *holdeth peace*. The competing reading is named in that verse's note.

Rule 17's ruling that a supplied lexical subject noun is `added` does not reach such a pronoun: that ruling governs an English noun answering to no morpheme at all, as `יָשְׁבוּ בָהֶּ` → *men shall dwell therein* is, and here a written nominal answers to it, so read whether the verse writes the referent before marking a supplied subject `added` or folding it into the predicate under rule 20. **But a morpheme already holding a pronoun of its own is not a home for a second one.** Where more than one morpheme in the verse denotes that referent, each takes only the English written for it, as rule 51 says of a waw and rule 43 of a spent preposition: the object suffix of `מְצָאנֻהוּ` above takes the *him* of *find him out* under rule 18, and the further *He* goes to `שַׁדַּי`. Count the ASV's realizations against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s. **And where the two realizations are not of the same kind, the head goes to the one writing the noun's own lexeme, whichever of them stands first.** The direction to head on the first English occurrence settles a tie between realizations of one kind — two *he*s, two *from*s, or a noun and the pronoun resuming it in that order — and it is not a preference for the phrase's left edge. Where the ASV realizes one written nominal both by a pronoun and by the word that writes its lexeme, rule 24 governs and the head is the lexeme-bearing word, exactly as rule 18 heads a twice-written suffix on the pronoun that realizes it directly rather than on the generic noun beside it, and as rule 31 keeps a head off a word the ASV supplied. This reaches a construct chain whose *nomen rectum* the ASV promotes to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's own relation as a possessive on the head noun: `בְּפֶה חָנֵף יַשְׁחִת רֵעֵהוּ` → *With* ***his*** *mouth* ***the godless man*** *destroyeth his neighbor* gives both *his* and *the godless man* to the one `חָנֵף`, headed on *godless*, while `פֶּה` keeps its own *mouth*, and `וּבְהַוַּת בֹּגְדִים יִלָּכֵדוּ` → *But* ***the treacherous*** *shall be taken in* ***their own*** *iniquity* divides the same way, headed on *treacherous*. Such a possessive is not `added` under rule 18's closing sentence and the promoted subject is not `added` under rule 17: a morpheme in the phrase answers to each, which is the count the paragraph above runs. Read which English word writes the lexeme before reaching for the first occurrence, since Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English writes the possessive before it, so the pronoun stands first as often as not. **But an expletive the ASV writes to fill a subject slot English cannot leave empty realizes no referent at all, whatever the verse writes.** Where the ASV extraposes a clausal subject the Hebrew writes — an infinitive phrase, or another clause the ASV renders in full further on — and puts an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand, the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and rule 20 governs it: it is its own `added` unit, while the predicate keeps the copula that rule gives it and the extraposed clause keeps its own English. `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → ***it*** *is an abomination to fools to depart from evil* leaves that *it* `added`, with *is an abomination* on the construct noun and *to depart* on the infinitive. What the sentences above place is a pronoun denoting a referent the verse names and the ASV has rendered by a word of its own, so read what the pronoun stands for before folding it into a written morpheme's unit: `וְעֵץ חַיִּים תַּאֲוָה בָאָה` → *when the desire cometh,* ***it*** *is a tree of life* gives its *it* to `תַּאֲוָה`, which the ASV has already written as *the desire*, and one chapter may write both shapes, as PRO.13.12 and PRO.13.19 do. **An interrogative particle or a negative whose scope covers coordinated clauses is read the same way.** Where the Hebrew writes `הֲ` or `לֹא` once in the first of two coordinated clauses and the ASV rewrites it at the head of the second, every occurrence belongs to that one morpheme's discontinuous unit, headed on the first: `הֲלוֹא מַחֲזֵה־שָׁוְא חֲזִיתֶם וּמִקְסַם כָזָב אֲמַרְתֶּם` → ***Have*** *ye* ***not*** *seen a false vision, and* ***have*** *ye* ***not*** *spoken a lying divination* gives both *have*s to the `הֲ` and both *not*s to the `לֹא`, while each verb keeps only its own subject pronoun and lexical verb. This is rule 55's reading of a subordinator the ASV rewrites over a coordinated clause, applied to the particle that governs one. The second occurrence is neither `added` under rule 30 nor folded into the second clause's verb under rule 17. **Where in that first clause the morpheme stands is no part of the condition, and neither is a repetition of the same English word.** What licenses the second occurrence is that the morpheme's scope reaches the second clause, so a negative predicating of a verbless clause governs a coordinated colon from the middle of the first as readily as from its head, and the ASV answers it with whatever word carries the negation where that colon opens — a *Nor* or a *neither* as readily as a second *not*. `שְׂאֵת פְּנֵי־רָשָׁע לֹא־טוֹב לְהַטּוֹת צַדִּיק בַּמִּשְׁפָּט` → *To respect the person of the wicked is* ***not*** *good,* ***Nor*** *to turn aside the righteous in judgment* gives both *not* and *Nor* to the one `לֹא`, headed on the first. Read the clause's scope rather than the morpheme's position, exactly as rule 51 reads a postposed *also*, and do not mark such a word `added` under rule 14's closing sentences because no conjunction stands in the second colon: what that count marks is a coordinator no morpheme answers to, and what distinguishes a *Nor* from a bare *and* is the negation the written negative is there to license, as rule 35 says in heading such a word on the negative. An ASV italic on such a word corroborates it and decides nothing, by rule 7. But read what is actually written before applying it: where the Hebrew gaps the morpheme in the second line and a waw stands there, and the ASV writes a single word carrying both the coordination and the negation, rule 35 governs and that word goes to the waw, as `לֹא עֲלִיתֶם ... וַתִּגְדְרוּ` → *Ye have not gone up ..., neither built up* leaves the *neither* to the waw alone; and where no conjunction morpheme stands in that colon at all, rule 35's fusion has no coordination to rest on and the distributed reading above governs.
amended.why: PRO.11.6 and PRO.11.9 are one construction the chapter met twice: the ASV promotes a construct chain's nomen rectum to the clause's English subject while writing the chain's relation as a possessive on the head noun, so one written noun is realized twice ('the treacherous ... their own iniquity', 'his mouth ... the godless man'). Rule 25's resumed-noun paragraph already places both realizations in the rectum's one discontinuous unit, and rule 19 already gives the relational expression to the rectum, so nothing new is needed there. What the rule had not considered is the head. Both of its worked examples put the lexeme-bearing word first, so 'headed on the first English occurrence' and rule 24's cross-language anchor coincide; PRO.11.9 pulls them apart, because Hebrew writes the possessor after its head noun while English fronts the possessive, leaving 'his' first and 'godless' second. Read literally the rule sends the head to 'his', which contradicts rule 24's own definition of a target head and rule 31's refusal to head on a word carrying no lexeme. The amendment states the boundary where it stands rather than adding a rule pointing back at it, and it closes the two related traps in the same breath: neither the fronted possessive nor the promoted subject is 'added', since a morpheme in the phrase answers to each. Both PRO.11 verses already head on the lexeme, so no patch follows from it; the correction is for the chapters after this one. Nothing else in rule 25 is changed.

report: Checked all 35 candidate lemma groups. Every multi-treatment bucket is licensed by what the ASV wrote or by a difference the source carries: the waw's And/But/then/that (rule 14, read off the ASV); the preposition be as a temporal subordinator where the clause is recast (11.7 'When ... dieth', 11.10 'when ... perish', 11.14 'Where') against an ordinary preposition elsewhere (11.4, 11.11, 11.22, 11.28); le unrepresented at 11.12 where the ASV writes the object bare (rule 40) and rendered wherever a word is written (11.19, 11.21, 11.24, 11.26, 11.29); akar a substantival subject at 11.29 and a predicate participle at 11.17, where the adjective is the substantive instead; min headed on 'than' for the comparative at 11.24 and on 'out' for the ablative at 11.8, both per rule 24.

Because the candidate table is blind to added units, I read the dump end to end for the 14 supplied runs. Their groupings satisfy rule 2's one-office test: the adjacent pair at 11.24 ('but' | 'it tendeth') is rightly two units, a connective standing beside a supplied subject-and-verb; 11.21 splits 'Though' from 'join' around rendered material; 11.15's 'for it' and 11.19's 'doeth it' are each one contiguous run doing one office.

Chapter-wide judgments verified consistent in every verse that raises them: the copula goes to the Hebrew predicate in all nine verbless clauses, including the three prepositional predicates (11.2 et, 11.14 be, 11.26 le) and the fronted comparison at 11.22; rule 31 heads move in both directions and are consistent (supplied generic noun, head on the lexeme, at 11.9, 11.16, 11.21; supplied modifier, head on the noun, at 11.14, 11.28); supplied determiners in construct chains follow rule 29's counting in all three shapes present (attributive rectum at 11.1, 11.16, 11.17, 11.18, 11.25; possessive rectum at 11.22; of-rectum throughout).

One gap surfaced rather than one split. PRO.11.6 and PRO.11.9 are the same construction handled identically: the ASV promotes a construct chain's nomen rectum to the clause's English subject while writing the genitive relation as a possessive, so one written noun is realized twice and both realizations sit in its discontinuous unit. At 11.9 the possessive 'his' stands first and the lexeme-bearing 'godless' second, which rule 25's 'headed on the first English occurrence' would wrongly send to 'his', against rule 24. Amended rule 25 accordingly; no verse needed patching, since both verses already head on the lexeme.

The three BSB disagreements (11.12 le, 11.15 ra, 11.28 hu) are the documented convention difference, where BSB attaches a morpheme to its phrase and the ASV's recasting leaves it no English word. None is an error and no accepted edge was changed.
